title: You can't subpoena a weight matrix

0:15 of the previous song is sampled in 1:03 of the next song.

chunks.content:
Music IP law is now quite established. If you sample someone's song without asking, it's up to that person to either ignore it or sue you.

But what if that sample doesn't show up in a song, but a response (text, image, video, audio) from a generative model with no deterministic way to trace the response back to a particular source in the training dataset?

At inference time, the original training data which is prebaked into the generator is scrambled and reprojected into completely new sentences. The opacity is structural to the final, trained model itself. But what isn't opaque is the ground truth the generator is based on.

> "Hm, our generative model produces videos that are kinda like James Cameron's Avatar. Was this model trained on Avatar?"

With many of the most popular LLM providers, we can only guess. AI companies may have stumbled into the perfect IP defense entirely by accident. In a typical IP suit, you have to show you own the original, that the defendant had access to it, and that what they produced is substantially similar to it. When the only user interface for the product is a stochastic generator, there's nothing to point to other than the probabilistic outputs it spits out.

If I have a long personal conversation with Claude, if they have a PII/PCI masking pipeline for all the conversation data (names anonymized like Sean -> Jim, credit card numbers masked ****), then at the end of this pipeline, they ask Claude "hey, can you generate a similar conversation, which reaches the same insights and uses similar wording, but tweak everything grammatically and sentence-structure-wise to make a meaningfully different copy". According to their terms of service, can they train a model on this "copy" data?

-----

**You can't subpoena a weight matrix.** And there's no deterministically traceable link between a training example and a specific model output. But you can subpoena the training dataset, and [courts already are](https://authorsguild.org/advocacy/artificial-intelligence/what-authors-need-to-know-about-the-anthropic-settlement/).

Generative models' responses come from 2 primary high-signal **ground truths**: the training dataset, and whatever context is passed as input at inference time.

If the model's ground truth (training data, feature data) is open source, we can trace an output back to original data with higher certainty. While you may not be able to prove a specific output came from a particular piece of training data, you can build a probabilistic argument that training on X influenced outputs that look like X. While an open dataset doesn't give you determinism, it does improve your confidence interval. A closed model confines us to observable behavior, where its internal structure and embedded biases [can only be inferred indirectly from outputs alone.](https://x.com/AnthropicAI/status/2025997928242811253)

You can only learn so much from shadows dancing on the wall. Sometimes, they distort reality, even if uninentional. At some point, you have to take a look at the primary sources.

> "Hm, our generative model seems to produce spot-on Warhol style paintings.", says Bill. Bill checks the training dataset, and finds that the model was trained on 10,000 samples of Andy Warhol paintings. He can say with pretty high confidence that the similarity of the paintings is caused by the Warhol samples.

> "Hm our generative model produces songs really similar to Joga by Bjork when I say 'produce a hyperpop track'", says Bill. Bill checks the training dataset. No Bjork.

Sometimes, it's a coincidence.

> "Hm, our generative model produces prose that reads a lot like Philip K Dick's Ubik", says Bill. Bill checks the training dataset and Ubik isn't there. But 10,000 Reddit threads, Goodreads reviews, and literary essays about Ubik are. Did the model learn the book, or everything written about the book?

This is not a persuasive essay. This is an essay of musing.

Should companies be held liable if their model generates something in the style of Bjork, if they didn't train their model on Bjork but the user passes all of Post into the model? My answer: no, that's on the user.

Should companies be held liable if they train their model on protected IP? My (and the law's) answer: yes, they should.

Should companies be held liable if they train their model on a protected painting which was anonymously leaked on some blog? Probably. Now we're requiring every single piece of training data to have an extremely high-confidence source.

Is it difficult to prove based on inference outputs alone whether a model is trained on protected IP? Yes

Should IP law be based on ground truth data composition or output similarity? Is this just a semantic similarity problem? If so, what's the threshold?

chunks.content:
Passing an Amen Break into a generative model, the sample dissolves into billions of floating point numbers and gets reconstituted probabilistically at inference time. There's nothing to point at if you're just looking at the output of the model. So, why would we _just_ look at the outputs of the models? The opacity of the weight matrix does not eliminate the traceability of the data distribution that produced it.

It of course comes with a cost. To open source a training dataset means open sourcing a massive dump of (anonymized) conversation histories. Given the number of people using ChatGPT as a first stop before making a doctor's appointment, or a sounding board for financial decisions, or god forbid a confession booth for their deepest darkest secrets, asking users for consent to publish their conversations is not a small ask.
